newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Trading states face off at WTO disputes panel.
newsitem.headline: Trading states face off at WTO disputes panel.

text.p: Trading powers will face off at the World Trade Organisation on Wednesday in rows ranging from a U.S. ban on Asian shrimp imports to Hungarian farm export subsidies and Argentine restrictions on foreign footwear.

Also on the agenda for the first 1997 meeting of the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) is a U.S. report on how it is implementing a WTO panel decision last year that found its limits on petroleum imports were against open trade rules.

The United States, which itself is leading an assault through the DSB against what it sees as violations of accords in the 1994 world trade treaty, is seeking panels against Turkey and Argentina over film taxes and footwear.

Potentially the most explosive of the disputes because of its environmental implications is the shrimp case -- in which a U.S. ban on imports worth hundreds of millions of dollars is being challenged by Malaysia and Thailand.

The ban, introduced last summer but lifted for Thailand in November after five months, followed a decision by a U.S. court in favour of a group that complained many imported shrimps were caught with methods that killed sea turtles.
The New York Court of International Trade ruled that wild shrimps caught by ships not equipped with devices to protect sea turtles, an endangered species, could not be imported.

Thailand, among 56 other countries found by the court to be in violation of U.S. law on environmental protection, decided to press ahead with the case although the ban was lifted for Thai imports after Bangkok proved it was protecting turtles.

Thai officials argue that the principle of the measure was unfair because it applied domestic law to other countries -- a charge made against Washington by the European Union in another WTO case over the Helms-Burton law on investment in Cuba.

The complaint is being backed by Australia, whose trade minister Tim Fischer said on Tuesday his country supported environmental conservation but argued the U.S. stance ignored differing circumstances in prawn-harvesting regions.

U.S. environmental laws also lay at the heart of the petroleum case, brought in 1995 by Venezuela and Brazil against the United States over rules that set higher standards for imported reformulated gasoline than for the domestic product.
Washington accepted the adverse panel finding and pledged it would bring its rules into compliance. But both Venezuela and Brazil say they are not satisfied at progress in this direction.

The case was significant because it was the first to go through the new dispute procedure since the WTO's launch in 1995 to replace the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and implement tougher procedures in trade rows.

The case against Hungary is being brought in four separate complaints from the United States, Australia, Argentina and New Zealand. Trade officials said a single panel was likely to be created to look into the issue.

"The Hungarians seem to be trying to go back on the commitments they made on agricultural trade during the (1986-93) Uruguay Round," said one trade diplomat. "They apparently feel they made a mistake in their calculations."

Hungary, like three of its four critics, is a member of the so-called Cairns Group of farm produce exporters in the WTO but has failed to calm their concerns in bilateral discussions under the preliminary stages of the DSB procedure.

The United States, which has initiated 20 of the 64 disputes now registered by the body, is also seeking a panel to look into Argentina's measures restricting imports of footwear, textiles and clothing items.
It is also asking for a panel to determine whether taxation of revenue from the showing of foreign films fits WTO rules.
